title: Certified Robustness to Adversarial Examples with Differential Privacy (PixelDP)
authors: Mathias Lecuyer, Vaggelis Atlidakis, Roxana Geambasu, Daniel Hsu, Suman Jana

pages.title: From empirical to certified robustness
pages.subtitle: A defense that comes with a mathematical guarantee

blocks.html: Most defenses against adversarial examples are empirical: they make the known attacks fail, but offer no promise against the next, smarter attack. History shows these defenses get broken again and again. What we really want is a certified defense: a proof that no perturbation below some size can change the prediction, no matter how clever the attacker.

PixelDP delivers exactly that, and it does so with a surprising borrowed tool: differential privacy (DP). DP was invented to keep a single database record from swinging an analysis. PixelDP reuses the same mathematics to keep a single small change in the input pixels from swinging the network's output.

We draw a formal connection between robustness against adversarial examples and a definition from privacy: a function that is differentially private with respect to small input changes is provably stable, and that stability can be turned into a robustness certificate.

The result is a defense that scales to large networks and datasets (including ImageNet), works with standard architectures, and crucially gives a per-prediction certificate: for this specific input, the label is guaranteed not to change under any attack within radius $L$.

pages.title: Why empirical defenses keep failing
pages.subtitle: The arms race and how to step out of it

blocks.html: An adversarial example is an input $x' = x + \delta$ with $\|\delta\|_p$ tiny, crafted so the model's prediction flips. Empirical defenses raise the bar for current attacks but leave a residual question: is the model actually robust, or did we just fail to find the attack that breaks it?

A certified defense answers that question with a proof. For a given input it returns not only a label but a guaranteed radius $L$ such that every perturbation with $\|\delta\|_p \leq L$ leaves the prediction unchanged. No future attack within that ball can ever succeed.

Differential privacy bounds how much the output distribution of a randomized function can change when one input is perturbed slightly. PixelDP's insight: treat a bounded change in the input image like the 'one record change' in DP. If the network's scores are differentially private with respect to a norm-bounded change in the input, then those scores cannot move much, which means the argmax (the predicted class) is stable.

pages.title: Inject calibrated noise into the network
pages.subtitle: Making the score function differentially private

blocks.html: PixelDP turns an ordinary network into a randomized one by inserting a noise layer. Gaussian (or Laplace) noise is added at some point in the forward pass, calibrated so that the mapping from input to class scores satisfies $(\epsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy with respect to a change of size up to $L$ in the chosen input norm.

The amount of noise depends on the sensitivity of the network up to the noise layer: how much its pre-noise output can change when the input moves by $L$. Concretely, for Gaussian noise providing $(\epsilon,\delta)$-DP at attack bound $L$, the standard deviation scales like:

Here $\Delta$ is the sensitivity (how strongly a unit input change propagates to the noise layer). Read it plainly: a bigger guaranteed radius $L$, or a more sensitive network, demands more noise; a tighter privacy budget $\epsilon$ also demands more noise. Noise is the currency you spend to buy a stability guarantee.
At prediction time PixelDP runs the noisy network many times (Monte Carlo) on the same input and averages the scores, producing an expected score $\hat{E}[\,Q_k(x)\,]$ for each class $k$.

pages.title: From DP to a robustness certificate
pages.subtitle: The bound that does the work

blocks.html: Differential privacy comes with a so-called expected-output stability property. If a function's output is in $[0,1]$ and the function is $(\epsilon,\delta)$-DP for input changes up to $L$, then for any perturbation within that bound the expected score cannot jump by more than a controlled factor:

In words: the privacy guarantee literally caps how far each class score can drift when the attacker perturbs the input inside the $L$-ball. Now the certificate is simple. Let $k_1$ be the top class and $k_2$ the runner-up. The prediction is certified robust at this input if the top score, even after the worst allowed drop, still beats the runner-up even after its worst allowed rise:

When this inequality holds, no perturbation with $\|\delta\|_p \leq L$ can make $k_2$ overtake $k_1$. The label is provably locked in. If it fails, PixelDP simply abstains from certifying that input rather than making a false promise.
The certificate is per-prediction: the same model certifies some inputs and declines others. Robustness becomes a measurable quantity, not a hope.

pages.title: Making the bound trustworthy in practice
pages.subtitle: Monte Carlo estimation and confidence

blocks.html: Because the scores are estimated by sampling the noisy network, PixelDP cannot use the exact expectations; it uses empirical estimates. To stay sound, it computes confidence bounds (via Hoeffding's inequality) on each expected score and plugs the conservative ends into the certificate check. This guarantees the certificate holds with high probability even though the scores were sampled.

items: Lower-bound the top class's expected score.
Certify only if the conservative top still dominates the conservative runner-up under the DP drift bound.
More Monte Carlo samples tighten the bounds and certify more inputs.

blocks.html: The accuracy-robustness trade-off shows up as a noise knob: more noise yields a larger certified radius $L$ but lowers clean accuracy. PixelDP lets you dial this explicitly, with the guarantee always intact.

pages.title: Scales where prior certified defenses could not
pages.subtitle: ImageNet-scale certificates

blocks.html: Earlier certified defenses (based on exact verification or convex relaxations) were precise but did not scale much beyond small networks and datasets. PixelDP's noise-based approach is architecture-agnostic and cheap, so it certifies robustness on large models and on datasets up to ImageNet, a first at that scale.

items: Gives a genuine guarantee, not just empirical resistance to today's attacks.
Works as a wrapper around standard architectures with a single added noise layer.
Certificate is per-input, so you know exactly which predictions are provably safe.
Trades clean accuracy for certified radius via the noise level, transparently.

blocks.html: The lasting contribution is conceptual: PixelDP showed that differential privacy and adversarial robustness are two faces of the same stability requirement. This bridge seeded a whole line of work on randomized-smoothing certified defenses, which became one of the most reliable tools in adversarial ML.
